question: On 16 October 2025, the Commission announced its intention to extend the Erasmus+ programme to countries in the Maghreb and the Middle East, including Algeria and Syria.

This announcement raises serious concerns, as Algeria is stepping up its diplomatic attacks against France, refusing to take back dangerous or convicted Algerian nationals and repressing freedom of expression, as evidenced by the case of writer Boualem Sansal.

Meanwhile, the current Syrian regime stands accused of committing war crimes and serious abuses, particularly against the Alawite minority, and has links with terrorist organisations, such as Al-Qaeda.

This announcement therefore raises major security concerns, particularly with regard to visas and migration control, since academic mobility programmes can be used as a point of entry or means of circumventing the security measures applicable to third-country nationals.
At the same time, the Commission is maintaining its suspension of Hungarian institutions from the Erasmus+ programme in the name of the ‘rule of law’. 1.
How does the Commission justify such moral and political inconsistency towards Hungary?
In view of the migration risks that could result from opening up the Erasmus+ programme to unstable and hostile regimes, how does the Commission intend to guarantee the security of Member States?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.1.2026) Countries in the Maghreb and the Middle East are not associated to Erasmus+ and do not receive a dedicated budget.

Yet, higher education students from those regions continue to benefit from the already existing opportunities under the international dimension of Erasmus+ programme, funded by the Neighbourhood, Development and International Cooperation Instrument, which include short term student exchanges from any region in the world towards the EU.

The Pact for the Mediterranean1 promotes a comprehensive, whole-of-route and rights-based approach to migration and mobility, which includes pursuing an effective return and readmission policy. When applying for visas, including for study purposes, third-country nationals go through thorough security checks.

As part of the general conditions set out under Article 7 of Directive 2016/8012, where third-country nationals are considered to pose a threat to public security, they should not be admitted. The Commission is legally bound to ensuring that organisations and individuals that do not respect EU values, such as the rule of law or respect for human rights do not receive EU financial support.
EU financial rules include an exclusion ground under the Early Detection and Exclusion System for entities engaged in activities contrary to EU values relevant in the implementation of EU budget.

The suspension of Hungarian institutions from the Erasmus+ programme concerns only a limited number of institutions (governed by the so-called public interest trusts) and is based on the Council Implementing Decision (EU) 2022/25063 adopted on the basis of Regulation 2020/20924. The suspension is not aimed at Hungarian students and Hungary continues to receive the full Erasmus+ budget.

1 JOIN/2025/26 final (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=celex:52025JC0026). 2 OJ L 132, 21.5.2016, pp. 21–57 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2016/801/oj/eng). 3 OJ L 325, 20.12.2022, pp. 94–109 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dec_impl/2022/2506/oj/eng). 4 OJ L 433I, 22.12.2020, pp. 1–10 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2020/2092/oj/eng).
